analysis.one_liner: Bars FDA from penalizing tobacco retailers whose face-to-face sales follow state law.
analysis.headline: A bill with 40 cosponsors to shield tobacco retailers from FDA penalties died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the Food and Drug Administration from fining retailers who sell cigarettes or chewing tobacco in face-to-face transactions that comply with a state law banning sales to people under 18 or 19. Because nearly every state had such a law, this would have overridden the FDA's 1996 tobacco rules, which put federal checks on youth sales — like requiring photo ID from young-looking buyers. The bill never got a hearing and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Tobacco retailers (convenience stores, gas stations, tobacconists) would gain the most: in any state with its own underage-sales law, they could no longer face FDA enforcement for face-to-face sales that complied with that state law, eliminating the risk of a federal penalty on top of state penalties and exempting them from the FDA's stricter federal youth-access rules. Cigarette and smokeless tobacco manufacturers would benefit indirectly, because the FDA's 1996 youth-access rules were the main federal tool for shrinking underage sales, and blocking their enforcement at the counter protects sales volume.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services, acting through the FDA, from taking enforcement action against a retailer for a face-to-face sale of cigarettes or smokeless tobacco in a state that has its own law banning such sales to people under 18 or 19, as long as the sale follows state law [S2].

Under the bill's terms, any face-to-face sale legal under state law would be immune from FDA action, which would have prevented the FDA from enforcing its own, often stricter, federal youth-access rules — such as ID checks — against retailers in those states [S3].
The practical benefit for retailers is freedom from a second layer of federal penalties for sales that already pass state muster, which is the bill's stated rationale [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Teens and the public bear the cost through weaker enforcement against underage tobacco sales: the FDA's 1996 rules — adopted because underage smoking was a leading cause of preventable death — would have gone unenforced against retailers in any state with its own underage-sale law, leaving youth access to tobacco dependent entirely on state enforcement of varying rigor.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have blocked the FDA's federal youth-access rules — its uniform national checks on underage sales, such as photo-ID requirements for young-looking buyers and limits on vending machines — in any state that had its own underage-sales law, leaving those federal protections unenforceable against retailers [S3].

It would have made state law the only check on youth tobacco sales, with no federal backstop, even though the FDA had asserted jurisdiction over tobacco in 1996 precisely to reduce smoking among children (the FDA estimated thousands of children start smoking each day) — this is the honest cost a supporter would have to acknowledge.
A retailer who sold to a minor but was not caught under state law would face no federal consequence under this bill, weakening deterrence against the sales that most endanger young people [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's rationale — sparing compliant retailers a duplicate federal penalty for sales that already satisfy state law — has surface fairness for retailers. But the trade it makes is lopsided: it trades away the FDA's entire federal enforcement role at the retail counter, in every state with an underage-sales law, in exchange for relieving retailers of a penalty risk that existed only when they sold to minors. For ordinary people, especially teenagers, the cost of losing federal enforcement of youth-access rules outweighs the benefit of shielding retailers from FDA fines.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to a House committee and then to its health subcommittee, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ray LaHood introduced the bill on February 13, 1997, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day [S1, S5].
Forty members cosponsored it — 31 Republicans and 9 Democrats [S4].
On February 24, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where the record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill expired in subcommittee [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Teenagers and public health came out ahead: because the bill never became law, the FDA kept its authority to enforce federal youth-access rules against retailers. Tobacco retailers did not get the shield from federal penalties they sought.

for.name: Rep. Ray LaHood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar FDA penalties on retailers for face-to-face tobacco sales that follow state law

for.name: 40 House cosponsors (31 Republicans, 9 Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral (Subcommittee on Health and Environment)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action record for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split at decision time is unknown; sponsorship was bipartisan but tilted Republican, with 31 Republican and 9 Democratic cosponsors.

industries.industry: Tobacco retailers (convenience stores, gas stations, tobacco shops)
industries.note: The bill would have exempted retailers from FDA enforcement for face-to-face sales that comply with state law, freeing them from federal fines and from the FDA's stricter federal ID and access checks. Their gain comes directly at the expense of federal enforcement against sales to minors.

The FDA's 1996 youth-access rules were designed to shrink underage smoking, which over time means fewer new smokers and lower sales. Blocking FDA enforcement at the retail counter in states with their own laws protects manufacturers' sales volume without them doing anything.

industries.industry: State governments (as enforcers of underage-sales laws)
industries.note: The bill treats state law as sufficient and defers to state enforcement, which respects state authority. But it also leaves states holding the only check on youth tobacco sales, with no federal backstop if state enforcement is lax.
